Stage 3 · Grammar

When the future wears the present

One rule, five words: when, as soon as, before, after, until.

Read these four sentences. They all come from the recording later in this lesson.
  • When you arrive, the instructor will check your fitness level.
  • You’ll definitely need to reserve a place before you come.
  • I’ll get back to you as soon as I know.
  • I just need to check I can make those dates. Then I’ll call and book.
All four sentences are about the future. What tense comes after when, before and as soon as?
The two halves
The time clause — Present SimpleThe other half — futureWhat it means
When you arrive,the instructor will check your level.it will certainly happen
As soon as I know,I will call you.immediately after
Before you come,you will need to reserve a place.earlier than
After the course finishes,we are going to stay two more days.later than
Until the rain stops,we will wait in the hut.up to that moment
compare If it rains,the experience will be more exciting.maybe, maybe not
Put the five time words in order, from the earliest moment to the latest.

THE RULE. After when, as soon as, before, after, until use the Present Simple, even when you mean the future.

THE OTHER HALF. That half takes the future: will, going to, or an imperative.

WHEN OR IF? when = it will happen. if = it may happen. When I get home / If I get the job.

Not “when I will get home”, not “until she will come”.

Same rule as the first conditional in Lesson 25 — one future marker per sentence.

THE RULE. English does not put will twice in one sentence. When a sentence has a time half and a future half, the time half stays in the Present Simple: When the rain stops, we will go out. Both halves are about the future; only one of them shows it.

THE FIVE WORDS. when (at that moment) · as soon as (immediately after) · before (earlier) · after (later) · until (up to that moment, then stop).

WHEN OR IF? This is the choice learners get wrong most. When I finish work, I’ll call you — you are certain you will finish. If I finish early, I’ll call you — you are not certain. Same tenses, different certainty.

ORDER. Either half can come first. Comma only when the time half starts the sentence: As soon as I know, I’ll tell you. = I’ll tell you as soon as I know.

Three mistakes to watch: “when I will arrive” · “until she will come” · “After I will finish, I go home” (both halves wrong).

You met the same tense rule in Lesson 25 with if. Nothing new has happened to the verbs — only the linking word changed.

Full grammar reference — Present tenses in future time clauses

Form

Structurewhen / as soon as / before / after / until + present, will + plain verb
ExampleWhen I get home, I’ll call you.
Order can changeI’ll call you when I get home. (no comma)
NegativeUntil you finish, you can’t go out.
Present Perfect is possibleAs soon as I have finished, I’ll send it.

When and why we use it

  • After these time words English uses a present form for future meaning — the same rule as after if.
  • As soon as = immediately after. Until = up to that moment and not before.
  • Before and after follow the same rule: Before you sign, read it carefully.
  • The main clause is where will, might, can or the imperative lives.

Signal words

when · as soon as · before · after · until · once · the moment

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I’ll phone you when I will arrive. → … when I arrive.No will after when.
  • As soon as I will finish, I’ll go. → As soon as I finish, I’ll go.Same rule.
  • Until you won’t finish, you can’t go. → Until you finish, you can’t go.Until is already negative in meaning.
  • When I will be older… → When I am older…Present form after when.

Don’t confuse it with

When here means ‘at the time that’, not a question. In a question will is normal: When will you arrive?
